questions.question: How many bytes are in 1 MB when the decimal SI prefix is used?
questions.explanation: One decimal megabyte is exactly 1,000,000 bytes. One mebibyte, written MiB, is 1,048,576 bytes.

questions.question: A 1 MB wire payload contains 8,000,000 bits. What is its ideal serialization time at 40 Mb/s measured goodput?
questions.explanation: 8,000,000 bits divided by 40,000,000 bits/second is 0.2 seconds, or 200 ms.

questions.question: A modeled path needs two sequential round trips at 70 ms RTT, and serialization takes 90 ms. What is the planning lower bound for completion?
questions.explanation: Sequential path delay is 2 x 70 ms = 140 ms. Adding 90 ms serialization gives 230 ms before queueing, loss recovery, and application work.

questions.question: What does the bandwidth-delay product estimate?
options: The bytes that must be in flight to keep a path busy at the modeled rate
questions.explanation: Bandwidth-delay product is bandwidth multiplied by round-trip time. It estimates the amount of unacknowledged data needed in flight to fill the path.

questions.question: A cache hit rate rises from 50% to 95% while the number and size of client deliveries stay the same. Which capacity boundary is reduced most directly?
questions.explanation: A reusable cache hit avoids fetching the representation from origin. The edge still sends the response bytes to each client, so client-facing egress remains.

questions.question: Why should retry attempts be included in an egress model?
options: Retries make MB and MiB equal
Retries create more wire attempts than logical deliveries
questions.explanation: A logical delivery can be attempted more than once. Those additional attempts consume edge and sometimes origin bandwidth even when they do not create additional useful completions.
